## Simple explanation

Workflow orchestration coordinates a sequence of automated jobs, making sure
each step runs at the right time and that failures can be handled.

## Technical explanation

An orchestrator represents work as tasks or steps with dependencies and
execution policies. It may provide scheduling, retries, timeouts, state
tracking, resource allocation, and event triggers. Orchestration systems
usually coordinate work rather than perform every computation themselves.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

AI pipelines often combine data validation, training, evaluation, approval,
and deployment. Orchestration makes these dependencies explicit and helps
teams monitor long-running jobs, recover from transient errors, and avoid
unsafe transitions.

## How it works

Define tasks and dependency edges, configure triggers and retry policies, then
submit a run. The orchestrator schedules eligible tasks, records status, and
surfaces failures. Idempotency and durable outputs are important when a task
may be retried.

## Practical example

Schedule a daily training pipeline that validates incoming data, trains a
candidate model, evaluates it against fixed criteria, and requests approval
before deployment. Store each task's inputs and outputs so a retry does not
silently use different data.

## Common misconceptions

- Orchestration does not make tasks correct or idempotent; those properties
  must be designed into the tasks.
- A workflow succeeding only means its configured steps completed, not that
  the model meets product or safety requirements.
